chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Abu al-Faraj al-Qummi, from Mu'adh, the seller of silks, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'O Mu'adh! Have you become weak in trade, or have you become indifferent to it?' I said, 'I have not become weak in it, nor have I become indifferent to it.' He said: 'So what is the matter with you?' I said, 'We were awaiting a matter, and that was when Al-Walid was killed, and I had much wealth, and it was in my hand, and there was nothing for anyone upon me, and I did not see myself consuming it all until I die.' So he said: 'You are leaving it, and leaving it is a depletion of the intellect. Strive for your dependents, and beware that they should not be the ones striving for you.'

key_terms.السُّعَاة: Those who strive/work (or those who are worked for)
key_terms.الْوَلِيد: Al-Walid (referring to a specific historical figure, likely Al-Walid ibn Ubayd Allah or a contemporary context)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic perspective on hoarding wealth versus active trade and supporting dependents?
ai.summary: Recorded in al-Kafi’s chapter on commerce, this hadith highlights Imam al-Sadiq’s (peace be upon him) practical wisdom regarding the stagnation of capital during the political turmoil following the death of Caliph Al-Walid. The Imam identifies hoarding wealth as 'madhahat al-aql' (the depletion of intellect), suggesting that idle capital reflects a lack of strategic engagement with one's responsibilities. He urges Mu'adh to actively trade to support his family, emphasizing that productive labor is a religious duty to prevent dependents from becoming a burden.
